intro: Frank Lévy plays the Nocturne in D♭ major, Op. 27 No. 2, marked Lento sostenuto. Left-hand semiquavers run beneath three statements of the D♭ major melody, and the melody is varied at each statement and at times divided into two voices.

sections.label: A · Left-hand broken chords, then melody
sections.mNote: The left hand begins alone; the melody enters on F.

sections.label: B · Two voices in B♭ minor
sections.mNote: The right hand plays in thirds above continuing semiquavers.

sections.label: A′ · Opening melody over D♭ bass
sections.mNote: The opening melody returns, marked dolce.

sections.label: B′ · Duet on C♯ and E
sections.mNote: The paired melody modulates towards A major and C♯ minor.

sections.label: A″ · Third statement of the theme
sections.mNote: D♭ major returns; the right hand then plays ornamental flourishes.

sections.label: Coda · D♭ pedal beneath changing chords
sections.mNote: The bass holds D♭ while the upper notes descend.

relations.basis: The nocturne alternates returns and expansions of its opening melody; the first paired excerpt agrees with the return marked near 116 s. cues.title: Opening, left hand alone
cues.text: The left hand opens the nocturne alone, playing D♭ major arpeggios across the keyboard in groups of six semiquavers. The right hand enters in the next bar on F, marked dolce. Under its first phrase the bass returns repeatedly to D♭.
cues.evidence: Claude Debussy edition (1915), bars 1–4; Mutopia transcription: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=486
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Melody in thirds
cues.text: The melody, a single line until now, is doubled in thirds. B♭ enters in the bass and moves the harmony towards the relative minor. The right hand plays espressivo, and the left continues its wide-spaced semiquaver figures.
cues.evidence: Claude Debussy edition (1915), bars 10–13: paired right-hand notes and B♭-minor harmony. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=486
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Training and teaching career
cues.text: Lévy entered the Geneva Conservatory at fifteen and later studied with Maria Tipo and Leon Fleisher. He taught at Juilliard for thirteen years. In 2014 he joined Musopen’s project to record Chopin’s complete works.
cues.evidence: Frank Lévy’s San José State University biography documents his studies, Juilliard post (1995–2008) and 2014 Musopen collaboration: https://www.sjsu.edu/music/faculty-staff/directory/frank-levy.php

cues.title: Return of the opening F
cues.text: After the wandering harmonies, F returns above a deep D♭. The first melody starts again, a tempo and dolce. Its long notes soon take on more ornaments, including a very light run marked leggierissimo.
cues.evidence: Claude Debussy edition (1915), bars 26–33; leggierissimo at bar 32. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=486
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Change to A major, bars 33–34
cues.text: In bars 33–34, D♭ and F in the right hand become C♯ and E. The bass keeps the same sounding C♯, and an A♮ in the accompaniment changes the chord from D♭ major to A major.
cues.evidence: Claude Debussy edition (1915), bars 33–34: D♭-major harmony changes to A major over C♯, with C♯ and E in the right hand. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=486
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Third statement of the theme
cues.text: The opening melody returns over D♭. Its continuation now extends into a long written-out ornamental figure, a run of small notes in the right hand that rises to the upper register and descends again.
cues.evidence: Claude Debussy edition (1915), bars 46–52: third return and the extended ornamental figure at bars 51–52. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=486
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: D♭ pedal, bars 62–68
cues.text: The bass returns repeatedly to D♭. Above it the right hand plays a descending chain of paired figures, each starting high and falling. Chopin marks the passage dolcissimo, very sweetly.
cues.evidence: Claude Debussy edition (1915), bars 62–68: recurring D♭ bass, dolcissimo and descending paired figures. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=486
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Mendelssohn’s letter to Fanny, 1835
cues.text: In September 1835 Chopin played this nocturne at Friedrich Wieck’s house in Leipzig. Mendelssohn was there, and wrote to his sister Fanny about the “lovely new notturno”, a considerable part of which he had learnt by ear.
cues.evidence: Mendelssohn’s letter to Fanny after Chopin’s September 1835 visit, quoted in John Henken’s Los Angeles Philharmonic programme note: https://www.laphil.com/works/two-nocturnes-op-27

cues.title: Ascending sixths, bars 75–77
cues.text: Sixths ascend through two groups of seven. The marking is dolcissimo e diminuendo, very sweetly and growing softer. The passage ends on a D♭ major chord.
cues.evidence: Claude Debussy edition (1915), bars 75–77: ascending sixths in septuplets, dolcissimo e diminuendo, final D♭-major chord. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=486
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: B♭ minor duet in thirds
transitions.from: A · Left-hand broken chords, then melody
transitions.to: B · Two voices in B♭ minor
transitions.how: The D♭ major phrase ends on F. The bass moves to B♭ and the right hand adds D♭ below the F, so the new phrase begins in B♭ minor with two voices in thirds. Beneath them the left hand continues the same six-note figure. Chopin marks the duet espressivo.

transitions.title: A♭ resolves to D♭
transitions.from: B · Two voices in B♭ minor
transitions.to: A′ · Opening melody over D♭ bass
transitions.how: The bass reaches A♭, and with C and G♭ above it forms the dominant seventh of D♭. The right hand climbs towards F as the chord resolves onto a low D♭. The opening melody returns, marked a tempo and dolce, and the left-hand semiquavers continue without a break.

transitions.title: F falls to E
transitions.from: A′ · Opening melody over D♭ bass
transitions.to: B′ · Duet on C♯ and E
transitions.how: In bars 33–34 the duet’s D♭–F pair changes to C♯–E. D♭ and C♯ are the same key on the piano, so the lower note keeps its sounding pitch while F falls a semitone to E. A♮ enters the left-hand arpeggio and makes an A major chord over C♯. The paired melody continues above the semiquavers of the accompaniment.
transitions.evidence: Claude Debussy edition (1915), bars 33–34. The A-major chord over C♯ precedes the later C♯-minor passage. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=486

transitions.title: Falling run leads back to the melody
transitions.from: B′ · Duet on C♯ and E
transitions.to: A″ · Third statement of the theme
transitions.how: In bars 45–46 a right-hand run falls across the keyboard while the left hand reaches A♭ dominant-seventh harmony. The bass then drops to D♭, and the melody begins on F for the third time. The forceful accents of the preceding passage are followed by dolce.

transitions.title: D♭ held in the bass
transitions.from: A″ · Third statement of the theme
transitions.to: Coda · D♭ pedal beneath changing chords
transitions.how: In bars 61–65, the A♭ dominant harmony resolves onto D♭ in the bass. The right hand then plays a high D♭ that falls to G and continues downwards in similar pairs, marked dolcissimo. The chords change above a D♭ that is held underneath each of them. The left hand keeps moving, and its lowest note stays on D♭ throughout.

composer.born: 1 March 1810, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: Composer for the piano, known for music that drew on operatic singing and on the irregular accents of the mazurka.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832 Chopin, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist, played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. He had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers, and teaching soon supplied his living. For the rest of his life his profession depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from one concert city to the next; Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. The family moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
